title: Piano Concerto No. 5 in E-flat major, “Emperor”
hook: Written under French guns in 1809, it opens with the piano taking command.

painting.title: The Emperor Napoleon in His Study at the Tuileries
painting.pairingNote: The emperor whose army shelled Vienna while Beethoven was writing this concerto, painted in 1812, the year it was first heard there; the nickname “Emperor” was never Beethoven’s.

facts: Beethoven wrote the concerto in 1809, the year Napoleon’s army besieged and occupied Vienna. In July he wrote to his publisher that there was “nothing but drums, cannons, men, misery of all sorts” around him. The story goes that during the bombardment he sheltered in his brother’s cellar with pillows over his ears.
It is dedicated to Archduke Rudolf, a younger brother of the Austrian emperor and Beethoven’s pupil, friend and patron.

Beethoven had been the soloist in his earlier concertos, but by now his hearing was too poor for him to play this one. Friedrich Schneider gave the premiere in Leipzig on 28 November 1811; Beethoven’s pupil Carl Czerny played it in Vienna on 12 February 1812.

The nickname “Emperor” is not Beethoven’s and its origin is uncertain; it may come from his English publisher, Johann Baptist Cramer. Writers such as Donald Tovey think Beethoven, no friend of Napoleon’s conquests, would have disliked it.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a grand, martial opening movement led by the piano (I), a hushed hymn in a far-away key (II), a leaping dance that bursts in without a break (III).

movements.heading: Allegro
movements.summary: Instead of waiting for the orchestra to finish its introduction, the piano answers the very first chord with a sweeping solo. Three times. Only then does the orchestra begin the [[double-exposition|double exposition]] of a Classical concerto, with a proud, striding theme and a soft march. When the soloist returns, the two sides compete, interrupt each other and finally join forces. Beethoven even wrote out the [[cadenza|cadenza]] himself.

mainIdeas.name: The opening
mainIdeas.description: three huge orchestral chords, each answered by a burst of [[arpeggio|arpeggio]]s, [[trill|trill]]s and scales from the piano.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1
mainIdeas.description: a proud, striding tune, martial in the orchestra, gentle in the piano.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2
mainIdeas.description: a soft march, first in the minor in the strings, then in the major in the horns.

stops.hear: One huge chord from the orchestra; the piano answers with a sweep of rippling chords, trills and scales. Twice more
stops.happening: Three chords, three solos: the piano takes command before the orchestra has played a tune

stops.hear: The orchestra launches a proud, striding theme
Very quiet, a march in the strings, in the minor; then the horns play it softly in the major
The piano re-enters with a slow, rising scale, then plays Theme 1 softly and tenderly
Very soft and high, the piano plays the march in a far-away key
stops.happening: Theme 2 in B minor, a surprise key

stops.hear: The orchestra bursts in and plays the march loudly, in the expected key
The themes are broken up and passed between piano and orchestra
Piano and orchestra hurl heavy octaves and chords at each other
stops.happening: The battle at the centre of the movement

stops.hear: The great chords and piano solos return
The orchestra stops; the piano plays alone, but only briefly
stops.happening: The [[cadenza|cadenza]], written out by Beethoven, who told the soloist not to add one of their own

stops.hear: The horns join the piano quietly with the march tune

stops.label: Last 2 minutes
stops.hear: Piano and orchestra together, building to a firm ending in E-flat major

notice: Compare the first theme in the orchestra and in the piano. The orchestra marches; the piano sings the same tune softly.
At the cadenza, notice how quickly the horns come back in. Beethoven keeps the soloist on a short leash.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: A concert recording: Zimerman, Bernstein and the Vienna Philharmonic played the concerto in the Musikverein, Vienna, in September 1989, alongside Nos. 3 and 4. Bernstein died in October 1990; Zimerman recorded Nos. 1 and 2 in 1991, directing the orchestra from the keyboard. Bernstein takes the slow movement broadly: just over nine minutes, where many recordings take about seven and a half. On the Spotify album the concerto is tracks 13–15.

movements.heading: Adagio un poco mosso
movements.summary: A hushed hymn in B major, a key very far from the concerto’s E-flat. [[muted|muted]] strings play the hymn; the piano floats above them, then sings it itself. At the end the music sinks by a half-step, and the piano quietly tries out the theme of the finale before it bursts in.

mainIdeas.name: The hymn
mainIdeas.description: a slow, quiet melody for muted strings.

mainIdeas.name: The piano’s line
mainIdeas.description: a soft, falling thread of notes high above, like an improvisation.

stops.hear: Muted strings play a slow, hushed hymn
stops.happening: The theme, in B major, a world away from E-flat

stops.hear: The piano enters high up with a slow, falling line of soft notes
stops.happening: The piano answers the hymn rather than repeating it

stops.hear: The piano plays the hymn itself, in quiet chords
Flute, clarinet and bassoon take the hymn; the piano decorates it with soft, flowing notes
stops.happening: The theme in the woodwinds, the piano accompanying

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: A held note sinks by a half-step; the piano slowly sketches a new tune, hesitating
stops.happening: The bridge to the finale: the piano previews the rondo theme, and the next movement follows without a break ([[attacca|attacca]])

notice: Listen to the last half-minute. The piano plays the finale’s theme slowly, as if remembering it, and then the finale bursts in at full speed.

movements.heading: Rondo: Allegro ma non troppo
movements.summary: The piano leaps in with a dancing theme in six beats, and the orchestra repeats it with full force. A [[rondo|rondo]]: the theme keeps returning between other episodes, and in the middle it travels through three different keys. Near the end the music suddenly slows and quietens, leaving the piano alone with the timpani before the final rush.

mainIdeas.name: The rondo theme
mainIdeas.description: a leaping, dancing tune in six beats, with a lively, off-balance rhythm.

mainIdeas.name: The timpani
mainIdeas.description: a soft, steady tapping in the coda, under the piano’s last fragments.

stops.hear: The piano bursts in with a leaping, dancing theme; the orchestra repeats it loudly
Rippling runs in the piano and a lighter second tune
The leaping theme again, in the piano
The theme is taken through three different keys; then the piano ripples alone
stops.happening: The central episode, a [[development|development]] of the theme

stops.hear: The rondo theme returns in the home key
The music slows and quietens: the piano plays fragments of the theme over a soft, steady tapping from the timpani
stops.happening: Piano and timpani alone, the energy draining away

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: The piano rushes up the keyboard; the orchestra ends with loud chords

notice: Near the end, listen to the timpani. For a few bars only the piano and the drum are left, getting slower and quieter, before one last burst.

threads.title: The piano in command
threads.body: The soloist opens the concerto, leads the bridge into the finale and starts the rondo: this is a concerto in which the piano leads.

threads.title: Linked movements
threads.body: The slow movement does not end; it turns into the finale, with the piano trying out the new theme first.

threads.title: Far-away keys
threads.body: The slow movement is in B major, and in the first movement the piano plays the march in B minor: Beethoven keeps stepping just a half-step away from home.
